oil.summary: Crude sold off sharply on Tuesday, with WTI settling near $72.85 (-2.62%) and RBOB gasoline cratering 5.77% on the day, extending a brutal month-long rout of roughly 24% for the benchmark. The dominant driver is the U.S. granting Iran a 60-day sanctions waiver through 21 August, allowing crude flows to India and broader Asian markets and removing a significant supply-risk premium. Hormuz ambiguity persists — IOC failed to attract a single bid on a tanker tender, underscoring residual freight risk even as peace talks progress. Partially offsetting the bearish impulse: Trump signalled reimposition of Russian crude sanctions 'soon,' and Russia is weighing a full diesel export ban amid domestic refinery disruptions. Options markets price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting, reflecting deepening demand anxiety.
drivers: US grants 60-day Iran sanctions waiver, unlocking potential crude supply to India and Asia and deflating the geopolitical risk premium
Hormuz traffic remains erratic — IOC tanker tender drew zero bids, keeping freight risk elevated despite ceasefire talk
Countervailing sanction signals: Trump threatens to reimpose Russia oil sanctions; Russia mulls full diesel export ban amid domestic refinery strain

gas.summary: Natural gas markets diverged sharply by geography. Henry Hub edged down 0.98% on the day to $3.221/MMBtu but remains up 6.73% over the past month, supported in part by record U.S. LPG exports to India — which is replacing disrupted Middle East flows with American supply. TTF in Europe was nearly flat on the day at €41.855/MWh but is down 15.29% over the month, reflecting some easing of Hormuz-driven supply anxiety. Gas-specific headline flow was thin today; the most relevant cross-market dynamic remains India's pivot toward U.S. LNG and LPG as IOC struggles to secure tankers for Gulf cargoes. European battery storage installations projected to quadruple by 2030 (per SolarPower Europe) represent a medium-term structural headwind to gas-fired power demand.
drivers: India boosting U.S. LPG imports to a record high in June, substituting disrupted Middle East supply and supporting Henry Hub-linked export demand
TTF soft on the month as Iran sanctions waiver reduces European supply-shock fears, though Hormuz tanker market remains impaired
Europe's battery storage capacity set to quadruple by 2030, a structural long-term drag on gas demand in the power mix

power.summary: EU carbon (EUA) slipped 1.38% on the day to $75.93 but holds a 4.50% gain over the past month, a contrast to the sharp retreat in TTF (-15.29% over the month) that would normally weigh on carbon through reduced gas-burn economics. The U.S. suspension of Iran oil sanctions until 21 August — with nuclear inspectors returning — is the dominant macro backdrop, easing some of the energy security stress that had buoyed carbon in recent weeks. UK grid operator NESO confirmed sufficient electricity supply for winter despite Hormuz disruption, removing an acute scarcity narrative for British power. SolarPower Europe's forecast of quadrupling utility-scale battery storage by 2030 adds a longer-term bearish structural layer to carbon demand from the power sector.
drivers: EUA holding monthly gains despite falling TTF, suggesting carbon is pricing structural demand rather than near-term gas substitution
UK NESO confirms adequate winter electricity supply, removing an acute bullish catalyst tied to the Hormuz crisis
European battery storage set to quadruple by 2030 per SolarPower Europe, a medium-term headwind to fossil-fuel power demand and carbon burn
